body_text:
The Archimedean Property. For every real number
$x \in \mathbb{R}$, there exists a natural number
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $n > x$. Equivalently, for every
$\epsilon > 0$, there exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that
$0 < 1/n < \epsilon$.

*Proof*: Suppose for contradiction that $\mathbb{N}$ is bounded
above in $\mathbb{R}$. Since $\mathbb{N} \neq \emptyset$, the
Completeness Axiom guarantees that $\alpha = \sup(\mathbb{N})$
exists in $\mathbb{R}$. Since $\alpha - 1 < \alpha$, $\alpha - 1$
is not an upper bound for $\mathbb{N}$. Thus there exists some
$m \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $m > \alpha - 1$. Adding $1$ to both
sides gives $m + 1 > \alpha$. Since $m + 1 \in \mathbb{N}$, this
contradicts that $\alpha$ is an upper bound for $\mathbb{N}$.

Hence $\mathbb{N}$ is unbounded above in $\mathbb{R}$. The
Archimedean property rules out actual infinitesimals and actual
infinities in the standard real field.
